Previously reported cases suggest that some former league footballers experience dementia earlier than anticipated; although a prior study indicated a connection between professional football and dementia, those findings were inconclusive without further investigation in a larger group.
Justin Hardy/PA Media
The players in this study were all aged between 58 and 65. Through brain bank testing, two individuals in the group were diagnosed with CTE, while three others exhibited memory issues akin to those in dementia. Nearly half of the group, 48%, showed an identical brain pattern to CTE, and five percent were considered to have normal brains.
Three individuals diagnosed with CTE had played at a top level, with two of them having played professionally at various levels (across two clubs), another at a semi-professional level for three levels, and three only at grassroots level.
Cause of dementia
Two of the three with CTE were left with symptoms consistent with dementia and one was with mild cognitive impairment. In any specific case, the reason for CTE remains unclear, but research suggests that repeated mild head injuries might lead to brain tissue death, believed to result in dementia.

This included a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes, which is one of the risk factors associated with dementia, and a diagnosis of high blood pressure.
A member of the group had suffered three or more concussions and significant mid-brain injury, and is probably living with chronic traumatic encephalopathy and potentially early onset dementia, resulting in the player's death at 47 years old.
